div.p: The major histocompatibility complex (MHC) plays an important role in the immune response and may thus crucially affect an individual's fitness, relevant also for studies on evolutionary ecology and wildlife conservation. Detailed knowledge on the genomic organization, polymorphism and diversity of the MHC has a narrow taxonomic focus though and among macaques is only available for rhesus and long-tailed macaques-the species most commonly kept for biomedical research. The lack of data on wild populations is largely due to the difficulty of obtaining blood or tissue samples necessary for genotyping approaches. Here, we aimed at analyzing MHC-DRB from non-invasively collected fecal samples in wild Assamese macaques (Macaca assamensis), utilizing the MHC-DRB-STR (D6S2878) microsatellite marker. Due to the fecal DNA source incomplete genotypes occurred, which may be improved in the future by method refinement. We detected 28 distinct DRB-STR lengths in 43 individuals with individual genotypes containing 1-9 MHC-DRB-STRs and defined four haplotypes segregating between families in Mendelian fashion. Our results indicate that variability and diversity of MHC-DRB in Assamese macaques is comparable to that of other macaque species and importantly, that fecal samples can be used for non-invasive analysis of MHC genes after refinement of the applied methods, opening a number of opportunities for MHC research on natural populations. div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Research on the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) and its role in disease susceptibility and immune function has been largely focused on disease model organisms such as rodents or rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) [Bontrop & Watkins, 2005;de Groot et al., 2008;Doxiadis et al., 2001;Günther & Walter, 2001;Jordan & Bruford, 1998;Otting et al., 2002;Penn et al., 2002;Woelfing et al., 2009] but has become increasingly interesting also for the fields of conservation, evolutionary ecology and sexual selection. Being one of the most, if not the most variable gene complex in vertebrates [Piertney & Oliver, 2006], the MHC is considered a major factor of adaptive genetic variation, with many studies aiming at explaining the extensive polymorphism of MHC genes [Apanius et al., 1997;Meyer-Lucht & Sommer, 2005;Milinski, 2006;Piertney & Oliver, 2006] and the fitness consequences associated with variation in the MHC [Huchard et al., 2010;Sauermann et al., 2001;Sommer, 2005]. MHC related fitness consequences have been investigated in wild or semi free-ranging populations of non-model species with regard to for example reproduction [Knapp et al., 1996], kin recognition [Célérier et al., 2010], mate choice [Huchard et al., 2010;Paterson & Pemberton, 1997;Sauermann et al., 2001;Schwensow et al., 2008;Setchell et al., 2010;Westerdahl, 2004], parasite susceptibility [Lenz et al., 2009;Meyer-Lucht & Sommer, 2005;Paterson et al., 1998;Schad et al., 2012;Schad et al., 2005;Schwensow et al., 2007] and conservation [Becker et al., 2009;Gutierrez-Espeleta et al., 2001;Sommer, 2005;Ujvari & Belov, 2011]. Further studies may not only help to elucidate the evolutionary processes shaping MHC variability and diversity, but also aid in monitoring populations and genetic aspects of wildlife conservation.

For various reasons, non-human primates are especially intriguing subjects for studying evolution and genetic variability; being preferred study species, we have profound knowledge of many primate species and taxa concerning behavior, ecology and phylogenetic relationships. Primates show large inter-and intraspecific differences in social structure and organization and socio-ecology [Kappeler & van Schaik, 2002], which allows for comparative studies investigating the precise circumstances and evolutionary pressures that have shaped non-human primate species. Concerning the MHC, data on several taxa, for example lemurs [Huchard et al., 2012;Schad et al., 2005;Schwensow et al., 2007], marmosets [Antunes et al., 1998], macaques [de Groot et al., 2008;Sauermann et al., 2001], baboons [Huchard et al., 2006], chimpanzees [de Groot et al., 2009] and humans [see HLA database at http://www.ebi.ac.uk/ipd/imgt/hla/stats.html] are available. The genomic structure of the MHC is largely consistent among different primate species [Kelley et al., 2005] except for lemurs [Averdam et al., 2009], but interspecies differences and convergent evolution point to the influence of pathogens in shaping the MHC [Bontrop, 2006]. Consequently, data from wild and unmanaged populations and species not previously analyzed for their MHC may contribute to the general understanding of MHC evolution and MHC-fitness-relations. As many primate species are endangered [see the IUCN/SSC Primate Specialist Group: http://www.primate-sg. org/summary_primate_threat_status/], additional information will also be beneficial from a conservation point of view.

The MHC has been analyzed using tissue or blood samples [Froeschke & Sommer, 2012;Huchard et al., 2010;Paterson, 1998;Ploshnitsa et al., 2012], which are difficult to obtain from wild populations. In primates, invasive sampling is associated with trapping and often immobilization, which poses serious ethical considerations [Jolly et al., 2003;Sikes et al., 2011], especially when dealing with endangered species. To enhance feasibility of MHCgenotyping from non-invasively collected DNA samples, we aimed at analyzing the MHC-DRB locus of a natural population of wild Assamese macaques (Macaca assamensis) using DNA from fecal samples, utilizing the MHC-DRB-STR microsatellite marker: MHC-DRB is frequently used in studies concerning MHC-related fitness consequences [Froeschke & Sommer, 2005;Huchard et al., 2010;Schad et al., 2012;Schwensow et al., 2008] in non-human primates, being both polygenic (showing expansion and copy number variations), and polymorphic (showing allelic polymorphism). The MHC-DRB-STR microsatellite marker or D6S2878 is situated in the intron 2 sequence of MHC-DRB next to the most polymorphic exon 2 in all intron 2-exon 2 containing DRB genes [de Groot et al., 2008] and genotyping of this marker has been proven quick and reliable for assessing MHC-DRB variability and diversity in macaques [de Groot et al., 2008;Doxiadis et al., 2007]: DRB-STR patterns have been demonstrated to be associated with specific MHC-DRB haplotypes (containing specific DRB-exon 2 sequences) in the vast majority of cases in several primate species [long tailed macaques (M. fascicularis), de Groot et al., 2008, rhesus macaques and humans, Doxiadis et al., 2007, chimpanzees (Pan. troglodytes), de Groot et al., 2009], a pattern probably shared by all non-human primates.

Assamese macaques are a particularly interesting species for studying the MHC for two reasons: on the one hand, they have to our knowledge not yet been analyzed for MHC genetics or genomics, on the other, two aspects of their behavioral ecology make studying their MHC promising: First, the mating system of Assamese macaques deviates in important ways from the general baboon/macaque pattern. It is characterized by a lack of female estrous behavior and morphological or behavioral fertility signals that is coupled with an apparent inability of males to assess female fertile status, leading to pronounced possibility of female mate choice [Fürtbauer et al., 2011] with female preferences based on criteria other than rank [Fürtbauer et al., 2011;Ostner et al., in press], low mating skew and reproductive skew [Ostner et al., 2011;Schülke et al., 2010]. Since rank plays a lesser role in determining mating and reproductive success the role of the MHC in mate choice may be exacerbated. Second, the close phylogenetic relationships with the well-studied long-tailed and rhesus macaques together with their sympatric occurrence in mainland southeast Asia [Abegg & Thierry, 2002;Ziegler et al., 2007] may contribute to disentangling the influences of phylogeny versus that of similar pathogen pressures due to shared environment shaping the MHC.

div.head: Sample Collection
div.p: Fecal samples were available from 64 Assamese macaques from one habituated wild social group living in its natural environment at Phu Khieo Wildlife Sanctuary (16°5-0 35 0 N, 101°20 0 -55 0 E, 300-1,300 m a.s.l.), which is part of a contiguous system of protected areas, the 6,500 km 2 Western Isaan Forest Complex in Northeast Thailand (for detailed information on the study site see Schülke et al., 2011). Individualized sample collection was conducted between October 2006 and January 2008 and samples were stored in 100% ethanol for 24 hr and afterwards desiccated on silica and stored until extraction for up to 6 years. Paternity analyses [Schülke et al., 2010] identified 17 parent offspring triads and 2 mother-offspring pairs including 35 individuals (11 females, 6 males and 19 offspring).

div.head: Genetic Analyses
div.p: We extracted two independent samples per individual with the All-tissue DNA-Kit (Gen-Ial) following manufacturer's instructions. By cloning and sequencing seven successfully amplified samples we obtained 26 distinct Assamese macaque DRB-STR sequences that were aligned manually in Seaview version 4.4.0 [Gouy et al., 2010] and used to design a more specific Assamese macaque MHC-DRB-STR reverse primer allowing more successful amplification. For DRB-STR analysis we amplified the MHC-DRB-STR by hot start PCR in a 30 ml reaction volume containing 0.33 mM unlabeled forward primer Mamu-MHC-DRB-STR, 5 0 -TTC ACA GTG CAG CGG CGA GGT-3 0 and labeled reverse primer Mamu-MHC-DRB-STR, Hex-5 0 -ACA CCT GTG CCC TCA GAA CT-3 0 [de Groot et al., 2008] or the newly designed Mamu-MHC-DRB-STR-New, Fam-5 0 -ACR YCT GTG YYC TCA GAA CT 3 0 (all primers were purchased from Metabion, Martinsried, Germany), 1Â commercial PCR buffer (BioTherm™, Genecraft: Cologne, Germany) providing 1.5 mM MgCl 2 , 0.7 mg/ml Triton X-100 and 1.3 mg/ml BSA, 0.25 mM of each dNTP, 1U Taq DNA polymerase (BioTherm™ Taq DNA Polymerase, Genecraft) and 2 ml of the sample extract. Cycling conditions were an initial denaturation step at 94°C for 3 min followed by 50 cycles of 30 sec at 94°C, 30 sec at 50°C and 30 sec at 72°C and a final elongation step at 72°C for 5 min. Amplified DNA was analyzed on an ABI 3130xl capillary sequencer (Applied Biosciences) according to manufacturer's instructions, using Genemapper software (Applied Biosystems: Darmstadt, Germany).

div.head: Data Analyses
div.p: Of the 64 individuals, 43 were included in subsequent analysis based on three criteria. Twenty eight individuals were included based on "reliable genotypes": they shared more than two identical DRB-STRs in genotypes obtained from two independent samples and results from at least four independent successful DRB-STR analyses were available (see below). Fifteen additional individuals with known parent-offspring relationships were included despite not meeting the "reliable genotype" criteria to allow detailed family analyses. Consequently, we excluded 12 individuals from analysis because of genotype discrepancies between two samples and nine individuals with less than four successful independent DRB-STR analyses. To assess how many reactions are needed to obtain presumably complete genotypes we explored saturation curves plotting the number of each randomly chosen DRB-STR-analysis against the accumulated number of detected DRB-STRs for individuals with more than seven successful microsatellite analyses (N ¼ 14; Fig. 1). In only two individuals, more than four (six and seven reactions, respectively) reactions were necessary to detect the last DRB-STR, indicating that four reactions usually resulted in "reliable genotypes." We defined consensus genotypes for the 43 individuals, including only DRB-STRs that appeared clearly distinguishable in at least two independent analyses.
All statistical tests were performed in R, version 2.15.1 [R development core team, 2011], with level of acceptance set to 0.05.

The study was completely non-invasive and complied with the regulations of the involved institutions, the legal requirements of Germany and adhered to the principles of the American Society of Primatologists for the ethical treatment of primates. Approval and permission to conduct the

div.head: RESULTS
div.p: In 43 individuals (28 "reliable genotypes" and 15 additional family members) we detected 28 distinct DRB-STRs ranging from 153 to 284 basepairs (bps), detected in one to 21 individuals (Table I) by analyses with the Assamese macaque specific D6S2878 microsatellite primer. Each individual had 1-9 DRB-STRs (mean AE SD: 4.6 AE 1.9). Analyzing the segregation patterns of DRB-STRs between triads of parents and offspring defined by previous paternity analysis [Schülke et al., 2010;Sukmak et al., submitted for publication] by assigning offspring DRB-STR patterns to parent DRB-STR patterns where possible and identifying DRB-STRs that were always passed on from parent to offspring in combination, we defined four haplotypes that segregated in Mendelian fashion: DRB-STR lengths were (1) 153, 178, and 186 bps, (2) 166, 194, and 234 bps, (3) 178, 188, and 200 bps and (4) 184 and 210 bps, each haplotype appearing between four and nine times within the population (Table II), also in individuals without known family relations (Table III). As expected, the defined haplotypes do not or only partially explain the detected genotypes for most individuals, especially those without known family relations, due to the low number of individuals that could be assigned to family pedigrees. Several other DRB-STR combinations occur several times in the population, but without more extensive family data these cannot be defined as specific haplotypes yet.

In order to estimate how well our findings represented the overall MHC-variability in Assamese macaques we explored a saturation curve, plotting the number of each randomly chosen individual against the accumulated number of detected DRB-STR-lengths (Fig. 2). From the first to the 10th individual, 21 DRB-STRs were detected, whereas from the 30th to the 43rd individual only one new DRB-STR was found, indicating that most of the DRB-STRs in the study population were detected. Considering the individual saturation curves (Fig. 1) we found a significant positive correlation between the number of detected DRB-STRs and the number of analyses run for all individuals (Spearman rank correlation, n ¼ 43, R s ¼ 0.48, P < 0.001), but when considering only "reliable genotype" individuals, this correlation was no longer significant (Spearman rank correlation, n ¼ 28, R s ¼ 0.35, P ¼ 0.067), supporting the assumption that four independent analyses are sufficient and further repetitions will not detect new DRB-STRs.

Despite these generally consistent results especially for families consisting of "reliable genotypes" (Fig. 3), we found mismatches between parent and offspring genotypes in 13 out of 17 families, with DRB-STRs detected in offspring but not in either of the parents. In five of these families, only one mismatch occurred, but four families showed up to four or five mismatches. The average number of mismatches for all offspring of one individual was significantly negatively correlated with the number of parent DRB-STRs for mothers (N ¼ 11, R s ¼ À0.68, P < 0.05), but not the number of DRB-STRs for fathers where sample size is very low (N ¼ 6, R s ¼ À0.62, P ¼ 0.19). The sum of DRB-STRs of both parents was significantly negatively correlated with the mismatch number of the offspring (n ¼ 17, R s ¼ À0.65, P < 0.005), indicating a relationship between parental DRB-STR-diversity and mismatch number. More sophisticated statistical analyses on the relationship between parental genotypes and mismatches with the offspring were not possible due to the small sample size.

div.head: DISCUSSION
div.p: This preliminary study demonstrates that macaque MHC can be analyzed from fecal samples utilizing the MHC-DRB-STR, even for samples that have been preserved for a long time (up to 6 years). et al., 2008]. Also the length polymorphism in Assamese macaques is similar to that of other macaques: DRB-STR-lengths rhesus macaques:

153-293 bps [Doxiadis et al., 2007], long-tailed macaques 169-304 bps [de Groot et al., 2008], this study: 153-284 bps (Table IV). In accordance with other primates [Bontrop et al., 1999;de Groot et al., 2008;Doxiadis et al., 2006], our study indicates that the MHC-DRB gene has expanded in Assamese macaques and that copy-number-variations are found among individuals, with numbers of DRB- 153, 178, 186, 245, 158, 194, 200, 226, Haplotypes are depicted written eitherbold, italic or underlined and DRB-STRs belonging to haplotypes are sorted together (all other DRB-STRs are sorted by length). Note that in most individuals haplotypes do not explain the entire number of DRB-STRs present, so that haplotype definition needs to be considered as incomplete. In two cases within families, haplotypes might be present, but one mismatch occurs. These are depicted by a question mark and were not taken into account for haplotype frequencies.

STRs per haplotype ranging presumably from one to five (Table IV) compared to two to four in long-tailed, and two to six in rhesus macaques [de Groot et al., 2008]. Since DRB-STR diversity can vary between animals of different origin [de Groot et al., 2008], data on different populations will undoubtedly reveal larger variability of Assamese macaque MHC-DRB and additional DRB-STRs. We defined four haplotypes based on family segregation, but further data on multi-generation pedigreed families will be needed in order to assess the complete haplotype setup. In accordance with Lathuillière et al. [2001], a more specific primer and decreased annealing temperature led to better results in this study, leading to a set of 28 individuals with "reliable genotypes." However, parent-offspring mismatches occurred also, though to a lesser extent, in families consisting of "reliable genotype" individuals most likely due to incomplete parental genotypes. Consequently, it seems likely that MHC variability (allelic polymorphism) and possibly also diversity (copy-number variation) have been underestimated in the present study due to amplification failure of certain DRB-STRs in some individuals.

The explored overall saturation curve of DRB-STRs detected within the study population indicates that most of the DRB-STRs on the population level have been detected. This does not contradict the individual incomplete genotypes or family mismatches, as it reflects the number of DRB-STRs across individuals, whereas incomplete genotypes reflect undetected DRB-STRs within individuals. Individual saturation curves allow the conclusion that the occurrence of incomplete genotype is not caused by a too low number of analysis repetition, but need to be considered in the light of the current limitations of the method: Even with high analyses numbers, resulting individual genotypes can still be incomplete due to genotyping errors and allelic dropout, which are known problems when using non-invasive DNA samples [Fernando et al., 2003;Morin et al., 2001;Taberlet et al., 1999;Waits & Paetkau, 2005]. In our case, allelic dropout seemed to be rather sample than DRB-STR-specific, lengthdependent (Spearman rank correlation DRB-STRlength and frequency of detection, n ¼ 28, R s ¼ À0.31, P ¼ 0.11) or random, as some samples and even individuals could not be analyzed due to consistent amplification failure (data not shown), a pattern that seems to mirror the pattern in chimpanzee hair [Gagneux et al., 1997]. Furthermore, we observed the problem of preferential amplification of mainly the most frequent DRB-STRs (153 and 245 bps) generating too low signals for other, probably present DRB-STRs to be unambiguously detected. Primer inconsistencies and the resulting failure to detect specific alleles, as has been reported for STRs belonging to the DRB-6 lineage in rhesus macaques [de Groot et al., 2008], are also a possible major cause for the difficulty to amplify certain DRB-STRs; however, this does not explain why some DRB-STRs are reliably detected in offspring but not in some parent individuals.

Further improvements on the MHC genotyping method are needed for more reliable and complete analyses of MHC-DRB from fecal samples. Measures for future research are e.g. the generation of further Assamese macaque specific primers and the evaluation of the ideal sample storing method [see for example Fernando et al., 2003;Fike et al., 2004;Frantzen et al., 1998;Murphy et al., 2002], which can be species as well as locus dependent [pers. comm. C. Roos, see also Fike et al., 2004]. In contrast to Waits and Paetkau [2005] who stated that DNA concentration was the major predictor for PCR-success, DNA concentration measured spectrometrically (Nanodrop, PeqLab ND-1000) was not significantly correlated with genotyping success, measured as number of detected DRB-STRs (Spearman rank correlation, n ¼ 142, R s ¼ À0.03, P ¼ 0.72), in our study. The presence of PCR inhibitors [Fernando et al., 2003;Morin et al., 2001;Waits & Paetkau, 2005] should only play a minor role in this study as we performed a chloroform washing step in the extraction [Fernando et al., 2003] and added BSA to the PCR preparation, which should buffer possible inhibitors [Kohn & Wayne, 1997].

Validation of the results from fecal samples with blood or tissue samples will help estimating the genotyping error rates and reliability of the obtained results. Since it has been shown that microsatellites can reliably be analyzed from fecal samples with low error rates in Barbary macaques (Macaca sylvanus) [Lathuillière et al., 2001], we expect similar results in Assamese macaques. Better knowledge of Assamese macaque MHC-DRB-STR haplotypes could improve genotyping results by revealing marker DRB-STRs for haplotypes containing also DRB-STRs that are difficult to amplify. Considering future studies on potential pathogen resistance, information on the MHC-DRB exon 2 sequence will be vital, as it contains the highly variable antigen binding site and is thus connected with MHC specificity [Froeschke & Sommer, 2005;Meyer-Lucht & Sommer, 2005;Schwensow et al., 2007].

In conclusion, in this preliminary study we demonstrated that MHC genotyping from fecal samples utilizing the MHC-DRB-STR is possible despite some technical difficulties. These results show that fecal samples can pose an alternative to blood samples once ideal analysis conditions are established. Consequently, this approach holds potential for MHC connected research in wild, possibly even unhabituated populations.

figure.head: Fig. 1 .
figure.figDesc: Fig. 1. Saturation curves of detected DRB-STRs against number of DRB-STR analyses. For each individual, a different combination of symbols and lines were used. The saturation curves for number of different DRB-STRS detected against the number of successful DRB-STR analyses, calculated for individuals with eight or more successful STR analysis (N ¼ 14) indicated that four analyses per individuals are sufficient to detect complete genotypes. Analyses were randomly chosen. Note: Final DRB-STR number was five for six individuals and six for two individuals, resulting in overlapping lines.

figure.head: Fig. 2 .
figure.figDesc: Fig. 2. Saturation curves of detected DRB-STRs against number of individuals and DRB-STR analyses. The saturation curve for number of different DRB-STRs detected against the number of the respective individual drawn from the entire study population shows that after a rapid increase of detected DRB-STRs in the first few individuals the curve asymptotically approaches 28, with no new DRB-STRs detected through the last eight individuals. This indicates that most or all DRB-STRs across the study population have been detected. Individuals were randomly chosen (Note: Only datapoints for which new DRB-STRs were detected are shown).

figure.head: Fig. 3 .
figure.figDesc: Fig. 3. Exemplary pedigrees including eight Assamese macaques with known family relations and "reliable genotypes." Females are presented as circles, males as rectangles. DRB-STRs are depicted as defined haplotypes where possible. Paternal DRB-STRs and haplotypes are depicted bold, maternal DRB-STRs and haplotypes in italics, offspring DRB-STRs and haplotypes that can stem from either parent are both bold and in italics, one parent-offspring mismatch occurring in these pedigrees is underlined. The pedigrees demonstrate segregation of the MHC-DRB haplotypes (and DRB-STRs not yet assigned to haplotypes) in Mendelian fashion among known parent offspring triads.
